::: {.lead-question}
Given one top-down RGB photo of a crop field, can a model place **one laser point on each weed**, so that
most weeds are hit and almost no crop plants are?
:::

**Short answer — on the held-out test fields, yes, with a cost.**

## Question

**Why it matters.** A laser weeder destroys weeds without herbicide by heating the plant's growing point.
It needs a single aim point per weed — a bounding box is not enough, because the centre of a box around an
irregular weed can fall on bare soil or on the crop next to it. Every shot that lands on a crop damages
the harvest, so avoiding crops matters more than hitting every last weed.

**What is predicted, and when.** The prediction is made on the machine, frame by frame, as the camera passes
over the field. At that moment the only information is the **RGB image itself** — no species list, no stem
positions, no earlier frames.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Unit (one row)** | one plant instance (a weed or a crop) in one image; for the laser metrics, one shot |
| **Model output** | for every predicted weed: a pixel mask and one aim point (x, y) |
| **Target** | a shot is correct when its point lands inside a real weed and outside every crop |
| **Decision rule** | the laser fires only when the model is at least *X* sure a plant is a weed, and not within 20 px of a plant it thinks is a crop |
| **Main metrics** | share of weeds hit; share of shots that land on a crop; share of shots wasted on soil |

**Limits of the claim.** All evidence comes from offline photos: one main dataset recorded in European
fields with one camera, evaluated image by image. Nothing here is a field trial, says how much laser energy
kills a plant, or shows that the model works on other farms, crops or cameras. A small gallery of photos
from a different farm (Results) shows how quickly that can break.

## Data

**Main dataset: CropAndWeed** [@steininger2023cropandweed]. ${fmt(total("images"))} top-down RGB photos
(1920 × 1088 px, about 0.4 mm per pixel) of crop rows with weeds, recorded in
${fmt(total("sessions"))} recording sessions. It is one of the few public datasets that label **both crops and
weeds**, which this question needs: a weeds-only dataset cannot tell us whether the laser would hit a crop.

- **Annotations:** a box and stem position for every plant, plus a pixel mask that gives each pixel its
  species. We use the authors' own two-class variant *CropOrWeed2*: **Crop** (maize, sugar beet, soybean,
  sunflower, potato, pea, bean, pumpkin) and **Weed** (57 weed species).
- **Two recording sets:** *ave* = the Application set (real farm fields) and *vwg* = the Experimental set
  (test plots). Real fields are the harder, more realistic case.
- **Access limits:** non-commercial use only, and **no redistribution** of images or annotations. The data
  is downloaded from the official source in each run, and **no CropAndWeed photo appears on this site** —
  only statistics and model outputs.

**Key variables.**

| Variable | Level | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| RGB image (1920 × 1088) | image | the only model input |
| recording session (`ave-0543`, …) | image | grouping for the split and for confidence intervals |
| plant class: Crop / Weed / ignored | plant | target of the model |
| plant mask (pixels) | plant | training target; "did the shot land inside the plant?" |
| plant box, species id, stem point | plant | building masks; error analysis by size and species |
| predicted mask, class, confidence | prediction | laser decision (confidence threshold, crop gate) |
| shot point (x, y) and where it lands | shot | the main metrics |

**Quality issues that shape the method.**

1. **Plants outside the two classes.** ${fmt(total("ignored"))} annotated plants
   (${pct(total("ignored") / (total("ignored") + total("crop") + total("weed")))} of all) are species
   outside CropOrWeed2 or are labelled only "Vegetation" because the annotators could not identify them.
   They are kept as **ignore regions**: a prediction on them counts neither as right nor wrong.
2. **Masks are per class, not per plant.** Two touching weeds share one blob of "weed" pixels, but the laser
   needs one point per plant. *Preprocessing* explains how the plants are separated.
3. **Many plants are tiny.** Weeds outnumber crops about ${(total("weed") / total("crop")).toFixed(1)} to 1, and
   ${pct((dataset.sizes.Weed["0–16"] + dataset.sizes.Weed["16–24"]) / Object.values(dataset.sizes.Weed).reduce((a, b) => a + b))}
   of weeds are at most 24 px across (about 1 cm) — a few pixels once the image is shrunk for the network.
4. **Near-duplicate frames.** Consecutive photos in a session overlap heavily, so a random split would put
   almost the same image in training and test.
5. **Imbalanced crops.** A few crop species dominate (chart below); rare ones are harder to learn.

**Earlier dataset: CottonWeedDet12** [@lu2023cottonweeddet12; @dang2023yoloweeds]. Photos from US cotton
fields with boxes for 12 weed species (5,648 in the full release; a 2,391-image subset — 1,554 / 478 / 359 for
train / validation / test — was used). The first experiments used it, but it labels **no crops**, so
it can show weed finding but not crop safety. That gap is why the project moved to CropAndWeed; five of its
photos still appear in the gallery.

## Preprocessing

All steps are deterministic rules or come from the dataset itself; **no statistic is fitted on the data**, so
nothing can leak from validation or test into training.

1. **Labels → two classes.** Each species id is mapped to Crop or Weed with the official CropOrWeed2 table;
   unmapped species and "Vegetation" become ignore regions.
2. **Per-plant masks.** For each plant box, the mask is the class's pixels inside that box. Where that is
   ambiguous — two overlapping boxes of the same class, or a box with no class pixels — the image is passed to
   SAM 2.1 [@ravi2024sam2] with the box as a prompt, and SAM's mask is cut back to the class's pixels, so
   SAM can only split plants, never invent leaves. Each mask is stored as its largest outline (polygon).
3. **Split by recording session, before any model is trained.** Whole sessions go to train / validation /
   test (65 / 20 / 15 % of images, seed 42), so near-duplicate frames never cross splits. The split is
   fixed in [`configs/datasets/cropandweed.yaml`](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection/blob/main/configs/datasets/cropandweed.yaml) and rebuilt identically on every machine.
4. **Model input.** Images are resized to the model's input size (1024 or 1280 px wide, aspect kept) and
   scaled to 0–1 by dividing by 255 — a fixed rule, not a learned normalisation.
5. **Augmentation (training only).** Random mosaics, scale and colour jitter and horizontal flips;
   experiment 5 adds vertical flips and ±15° rotations, since a top-down photo is equally valid upside down.

**Who sees which split.** Training uses *train* only. *Validation* picks the best training epoch, the model
and the laser's confidence threshold. *Test* is used once, at the very end (Evaluation).

## Baseline and methods

### Baseline: "every green blob is a weed"

Without machine learning, a weeder could aim at anything green. The baseline computes the vegetation index
ExG − ExR [@meyer2008exgr] on brightness-normalised colours and keeps pixels where it is positive (its
published threshold, no tuning), cleans specks with a 3 × 3 opening, and treats **every connected blob of at
least 64 px** (8 × 8, smaller than the smallest labelled plants) as a weed, aimed at with the same point
method as the model. It cannot tell crops from weeds, so it has no crop safety gate. If a trained model is
worth having, it must beat this on crop safety without losing too many weeds.

The textbook ExG index with an Otsu threshold [@woebbecke1995exg] was tried first, on two validation images
only: the greenish tint of the soil in these photos turned it into hundreds of soil fragments per image, so
the published ExG − ExR rule replaced it.

### Model: YOLO11s-seg instance segmentation

YOLO11s-seg [@jocher2024yolo11] is a one-stage instance-segmentation network (10 M parameters). For every
detected plant it predicts a box, a class score (Crop / Weed) and 32 mask coefficients that are combined with
shared prototype masks into a pixel mask. It starts from weights pretrained on everyday photos (COCO) and is
fine-tuned on CropAndWeed.

- **Objective:** a sum of box-regression loss, class loss (binary cross-entropy) and per-pixel mask loss,
  minimised with AdamW for up to 80 epochs; training stops early when validation accuracy has not improved
  for 20 epochs, and the best validation epoch is kept.
- **Why this method:** the laser needs one point *per plant*, so plain semantic segmentation (one class per
  pixel) is not enough, and a box alone puts the aim point off the plant. A one-stage model runs in real time
  on a modest GPU, unlike two-stage models such as Mask R-CNN [@he2017maskrcnn].
- **Assumptions:** a top-down view at a fixed height, plants visible (not hidden under leaves), labels that are
  right on average, and test fields that look like training fields. The gallery tests the last one.
- **Three trained candidates:** exp 3 at 1024 px input, exp 4 at 1280 px (small weeds get more pixels),
  exp 5 at 1280 px with vertical flips and rotations. A fourth run at full 1920 px did not finish in time.

### From mask to laser point

The aim point is the mask pixel that maximises *(distance to the mask's edge) × (a Gaussian around the mask's
centre, width = half the plant's radius)*: it always lies inside the plant, near its centre, and not on a
thin leaf tip. Simpler rules fail in predictable ways — the centre of mass can fall between the leaves of a
star-shaped weed, and the box centre can fall on soil.

### Crop safety gate

A shot is vetoed when its point lies within **20 px (about 8 mm)** of a plant the model predicts as a crop —
roughly the laser spot radius plus aiming error. The gate can only protect crops the model actually
recognises; the Errors section shows what that means in practice.

## Evaluation

### Split and protocol

The split is fixed before any model is trained: whole recording sessions go to train (65 %), validation
(20 %) or test (15 %), so near-duplicate frames never appear on both sides. Then:

1. **Train** on *train* only. Ultralytics keeps the epoch with the best validation mask accuracy.
2. **Choose on validation.** Every candidate (exp 3, 4, 5) is run once on the 1,609 validation images, and
   every predicted weed down to confidence 0.05 is saved with where its aim point lands. Any confidence
   threshold can then be evaluated offline, without re-running the model.
3. **The rule, fixed before looking at the validation numbers:** for each candidate, the threshold with the **most
   weeds hit while at most 2 % of shots land on crops**; the final model is the candidate whose best
   threshold hits the most weeds (ties: the faster model).
4. **Test once**, for the final model at its chosen threshold and for the baseline. Test results are never
   used to change anything.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**What changed after redoing the choices on validation.** During development, test results were inspected
after each experiment, and exp 5 at threshold 0.15 looked best. To keep the test set clean, all choices were
redone on validation with the rule above, and test was re-run only for the final setup. The redo **changed
both choices**: exp 4 at threshold 0.05. The image size and augmentation experiments themselves were also
planned after looking at test results; that history is a limitation, not something the redo can erase.
:::

### Metrics

| Metric | Definition | Why it matters for a laser weeder |
|---|---|---|
| **Weeds hit** | share of real weeds with at least one fired shot inside their mask | weeds left alive keep competing with the crop |
| **Shots on crops** | share of fired shots that land inside a crop plant | each one damages the harvest — the costly error |
| **Shots on soil** | share of fired shots that land on neither a weed nor a crop | wasted laser time; harmless to the crop |
| **Shot precision** | share of fired shots that land inside a weed | 1 − crops − soil |
| Mask mAP50-95 | standard instance-segmentation accuracy on validation | secondary: how good the masks are, independent of the laser |
| Inference time | ms per 1920 × 1088 image, one Tesla T4 GPU | the machine must keep up with its driving speed |

Shots on plants that are marked "ignore" (unidentified plants) are left out of every count. Uncertainty:
95 % intervals come from **resampling whole recording sessions** (2,000 bootstrap draws), because images of
one session are not independent.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  title: "Why the rule picks the lowest threshold: shots on crops rise with the threshold",
  width: Math.min(width, 760), height: 220, marginLeft: 50, grid: true,
  x: {label: "confidence threshold", domain: [0.05, 0.95]}, y: {label: "shots on crops", tickFormat: ".1%", domain: [0, 0.03]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([curves.max_crop_share], {stroke: CROP, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.text([{x: 0.93, y: curves.max_crop_share}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: () => "2 % limit", dy: -8, fill: CROP, textAnchor: "end"}),
    Plot.line(curve, {x: "threshold", y: "crop_shot_share", stroke: greys[0]}),
    Plot.ruleX([thr], {stroke: SOIL})
  ]
})
```

**Reading the curves.** Lowering the threshold fires at more weeds, but also lets more uncertain *crop*
predictions reach the safety gate, which then vetoes more shots near crops. So the share of shots on crops
*falls* as the threshold falls (about 1 % at 0.05, above 2 % only around 0.5–0.7). The 2 % rule therefore
never stops the threshold from going down, and **the optimum sits at 0.05, the lowest value evaluated** —
an even lower threshold might score higher still. What the rule does not price is waste: at 0.05 more than a
quarter of shots hit bare soil, against about 16 % at 0.25. A real machine might accept fewer weeds hit for
less wasted laser time; the slider shows that trade-off directly.

```{ojs}
${pct(test.model.crop_shot_share)} of shots on crops (CI ${ci(test.model.ci.crop_shot_share)}) and
```

```{ojs}
<thead><tr><th>Test, ${fmt(test.num_images)} images</th><th>Weeds hit</th><th>Shots on crops</th><th>Shots on soil</th><th>Shot precision</th><th>Shots fired</th></tr></thead>

<td>${pct(test.model.crop_shot_share)}<br><span class="muted">${ci(test.model.ci.crop_shot_share)}</span></td><td>${pct(test.model.soil_shot_share)}</td><td>${pct(test.model.shot_precision)}</td><td>${fmt(test.model.shots)}</td></tr>
<tr><td>Baseline: every green blob</td><td>${pct(test.baseline.weed_hit_rate)}<br><span class="muted">${ci(test.baseline.ci.weed_hit_rate)}</span></td>
<td>${pct(test.baseline.crop_shot_share)}<br><span class="muted">${ci(test.baseline.ci.crop_shot_share)}</span></td><td>${pct(test.baseline.soil_shot_share)}</td><td>${pct(test.baseline.shot_precision)}</td><td>${fmt(test.baseline.shots)}</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>`
```

The model hits more weeds than the baseline **and** puts about 20 times fewer shots on crops. The baseline
is not useless — most weeds are green blobs — but it cannot tell a crop from a weed, so roughly one shot in
four lands on the crop.

### Did the final model overfit?

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const w = Math.min(width, 760) / 2 - 10
  const loss = training.history.flatMap(h => [{epoch: h.epoch, value: h.train_seg, series: "train"}, {epoch: h.epoch, value: h.val_seg, series: "validation"}])
  const left = Plot.plot({title: "Mask loss (lower is better)", width: w, height: 230, grid: true, marginLeft: 40,
    x: {label: "epoch"}, y: {label: null}, color: {domain: ["train", "validation"], range: [greys[1], greys[0]], legend: true},
    marks: [Plot.lineY(loss, {x: "epoch", y: "value", stroke: "series"}), Plot.ruleX([training.best_epoch], {stroke: SOIL, strokeDasharray: "2,2"})]})
  const right = Plot.plot({title: "Validation mask mAP50-95 (higher is better)", width: w, height: 230, grid: true, marginLeft: 45,
    x: {label: "epoch"}, y: {label: null},
    marks: [Plot.lineY(training.history, {x: "epoch", y: "val_map50_95", stroke: greys[0]}),
            Plot.ruleX([training.best_epoch], {stroke: SOIL, strokeDasharray: "2,2"}),
            Plot.text([{x: training.best_epoch}], {x: "x", frameAnchor: "bottom", dy: -6, text: () => "kept epoch", fill: "#5f6662"})]})
  return html`<div style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:20px">${left}${right}</div>`
}
```

Validation loss stops improving around epoch 50 while training loss keeps falling, and validation mask
accuracy plateaus; the kept weights are from epoch ${training.best_epoch} of ${training.epochs}. A development-time
check (not reproduced in the repository; it used local test images) scored exp 5 the same way on 297 training
and 297 test images: large weeds were found far more often on training images than on new ones (95 % vs 82 %:
overfitting), while weeds under 24 px were missed even on training images (71 % vs 66 %) — pointing to a
resolution limit rather than a lack of data. That is why the 1920 px run was attempted.

### Gallery: photos the site is allowed to show

CropAndWeed photos cannot be published, so the gallery uses two openly licensed datasets, **five random
photos each (seed 0)**. Click a photo: the raw image on the left, the model's output on the right —
**white outline = weed, light fill = crop**, laser marks **green = hit a weed**, **red = hit a crop**, grey =
soil, hollow grey circle = shot vetoed by the crop gate.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof pick = {
  const wrap = html`<div class="thumbs" role="group" aria-label="Gallery photos">${gallery.map((g, i) =>
    html`<button type="button" title="${g.dataset}"><img src="${g.raw}" alt="${g.dataset}, photo ${i + 1}" loading="lazy"></button>`)}</div>`
  const buttons = [...wrap.querySelectorAll("button")]
  const select = i => {
    wrap.value = i
    buttons.forEach((b, j) => b.setAttribute("aria-pressed", String(j === i)))
    wrap.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}))
  }
  buttons.forEach((b, i) => b.addEventListener("click", () => select(i)))
  wrap.value = 0
  buttons.forEach((b, j) => b.setAttribute("aria-pressed", String(j === 0)))
  return wrap
}
viewof showGt = {
  const label = html`<label style="display:inline-flex;gap:.5rem;align-items:center;cursor:pointer">
    <input type="checkbox"> Show the hand-drawn ground truth instead of the model output</label>`
  const box = label.querySelector("input")
  label.value = false
  // runs on the checkbox before its native "input" event bubbles to the label, where Observable reads the value
  box.addEventListener("input", () => { label.value = box.checked })
  return label
}
```

```{ojs}

    : html`<span class="hit">${g.weeds_hit} of ${g.weeds} weeds hit</span> · ${g.soil_shots} soil shots`
  return html`<div class="viewer">
    <figure><img src="${g.raw}" alt="Raw photo"><figcaption>Raw photo</figcaption></figure>
    <figure><img src="${showGt ? g.gt : g.output}" alt="${showGt ? "Ground truth" : "Model output"}">

  </div>
  <p style="margin-top:.5rem">${summary}<br><span class="muted">${g.dataset} (${g.licence}, <a href="${g.attribution_url}">source</a>). ${g.note}</span></p>`
}
```

### Earlier experiments (CottonWeedDet12, weeds only)

| Experiment | Model | Mask mAP50-95 | Weeds hit | Shot precision |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| exp 1 | YOLO11n-seg, 640 px | 0.812 | 92.5 % | 94.3 % |
| exp 2 | YOLO11s-seg, 640 px | 0.825 | 92.3 % | 92.7 % |

Both use SAM masks made from the dataset's boxes, threshold 0.25, measured on CottonWeedDet12's own test
split during development. That test split's labels were partly corrected by reviewing the first model's own
test predictions (52 weeds added, 35 marked unsure, 2 removed), which flatters these numbers. They show that weed finding works on a simpler dataset with large, isolated
weeds, but say nothing about crops — which is why the project moved to CropAndWeed. Full outputs are in the
repository ([`experiments/`](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection/tree/main/experiments/), `results/comparison.csv`).

## Errors

All numbers below are for the final model on the **test** images at threshold ${errors.threshold.toFixed(2)}. CropAndWeed photos
cannot be shown, so errors are described by type and counted; the gallery shows the same kinds of errors
on publishable photos. Plant size here is the square root of the **mask** area, which is much smaller than the
**box** size used in *Data* (a plant's leaves fill only part of its box), so the same bin labels hold different
plants in the two charts.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
sizeOrder = ["0–16", "16–24", "24–32", "32–48", "48–64", "64–128", "128+"]
Plot.plot({
  title: "Weeds hit by plant size (sqrt of mask area, px; ~0.4 mm per px)",
  width: Math.min(width, 760), height: 240, marginLeft: 50,
  x: {label: "weed size (px)", domain: sizeOrder}, y: {label: "weeds hit", tickFormat: "%", domain: [0, 1], grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.barY(sizeOrder.map(k => ({bin: k, ...errors.by_size[k]})), {x: "bin", y: "rate", fill: greys[0],
      title: d => `${d.bin} px: ${d.hit} of ${d.weeds} weeds hit (${pct(d.rate)})`}),
    Plot.text(sizeOrder.map(k => ({bin: k, ...errors.by_size[k]})), {x: "bin", y: "rate", text: d => `n=${fmt(d.weeds)}`, dy: -8}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const tiny = errors.by_size["0–16"], set = errors.by_set
  const sp = Object.entries(errors.crop_shots_by_species)
  const top = errors.top_sessions
  return md`1. **Tiny weeds are missed.** Weeds under 16 px (≈ 6 mm) are hit ${pct(tiny.rate)} of the time,
against 87–92 % for larger ones; they make up ${pct(tiny.weeds / Object.values(errors.by_size).reduce((s, d) => s + d.weeds, 0), 0)}
of all test weeds and ${pct((tiny.weeds - tiny.hit) / errors.missed_weeds, 0)} of the ${fmt(errors.missed_weeds)} missed ones.
At 1280 px input a 16 px plant shrinks to about 11 px.
2. **Real fields are harder than test plots:** ${pct(set["Real fields (ave)"].rate)} of weeds hit on real fields
vs ${pct(set["Test plots (vwg)"].rate)} on test plots.
3. **Crop shots come from crops the model does not recognise.** By construction, a fired shot that lands on a
crop means no crop prediction (at the threshold) was within 20 px — the gate cannot protect a crop the model
thinks is a weed or does not see. Crop shots per 100 test plants of each species:
${sp.map(([k, v]) => `${k} ${v.per_100_plants.toFixed(1)}`).join(" · ")}. **Sunflower** seedlings, broad-leaved
like many weeds, are shot most often.
4. **Crop shots are concentrated:** the top recording session alone (${top[0].session}; in a development-time look
at the annotations, very small soybean seedlings, median box ≈ 29 px vs ≈ 63 px for training soybeans) causes ${top[0].crop_shots} of ${errors.total_crop_shots}
crop shots, the top three ${top.slice(0, 3).reduce((s, d) => s + d.crop_shots, 0)}. A single unusual field can
dominate the safety metric — one reason the confidence interval for crop shots is wide.
5. **Soil shots (${pct(test.model.soil_shot_share, 0)}).** Mostly false detections at low confidence; some may be
real but unlabelled seedlings, which the data cannot tell apart.`
}
```

## Limitations

- **The test set was looked at during development.** Image size, augmentation and the early threshold were
  planned after seeing test results. The final model and threshold were re-chosen on validation, and test was
  used once afterwards, but the experiment history itself was influenced by test.
- **Some choices were never tuned on validation:** the aim-point method and the 20 px crop margin were fixed
  during development from geometry and test-set inspection.
- **The chosen threshold sits at the edge of the explored range (0.05)**, and the 2 % rule ignores wasted
  soil shots. A different but equally defensible rule (for example a cap on soil shots) would choose a higher
  threshold and hit fewer weeds.
- **One dataset, one camera.** CropAndWeed comes from European fields with one camera setup; the Sugar Beets
  gallery shows a large drop on a new farm and camera. No claim is made for other crops, regions or machines.
- **One training run per configuration.** Seeds were not repeated, so differences between experiments
  include training noise; the paired bootstrap covers sampling of fields, not of training runs.
- **Labels are imperfect.** Tiny plants have rough outlines; 30 % of annotated plants are outside the two
  classes and ignored; per-plant masks for touching plants come partly from SAM.
- **Offline image metrics only.** No field trial, no laser physics, no motion blur or timing. A shot "inside
  the mask" is assumed to kill the weed.
- **The 1920 px run did not finish** (out of GPU memory, then out of time), so the resolution question is open.
- **Prediction, not causation.** The analysis shows *where* the model fails (small plants, sunflower, one
  soybean field); it does not prove *why* — size, appearance and field conditions are entangled.

## Conclusion

On held-out CropAndWeed test fields, an instance-segmentation model with a crop safety gate hits about
**85 %** of weeds while putting about **1 %** of its shots on crops — far safer than aiming at every green
blob, which hits fewer weeds and puts almost a quarter of its shots on crops. The price is waste: at the
chosen threshold more than a quarter of shots land on bare soil, and the threshold choice depends on how one
values wasted shots against missed weeds. The remaining failures are tiny weeds and crops the model does not
recognise (sunflower, very young soybean), and the model does not transfer to a new farm and camera without
new data. The next steps would be full-resolution input for small weeds, more varied training fields, and a
selection rule that prices soil shots explicitly.

## Reproduce

Everything needed to check these numbers is in the [repository](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection);
its [README](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection#readme) has the full setup.

| Step | Command / file |
|---|---|
| Environment | Python 3.12, `pip install -r requirements.txt`, `python -m pytest` |
| Data access | `python scripts/convert_cropandweed.py --download --src data/raw/cropandweed_src --out data/raw/cropandweed` (official source; licence forbids redistribution) |
| Exact split | `configs/datasets/cropandweed.yaml`: grouped by session (`^[a-z]+-\d{4}`), 65/20/15, seed 42 |
| Preprocessing | `python scripts/prepare_data.py --dataset configs/datasets/cropandweed.yaml` ([`src/data/prepare.py`](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection/blob/main/src/data/prepare.py)) |
| Training (Kaggle, 2 × T4) | `python scripts/run_experiment.py --config configs/experiments/<exp>.yaml` ([configs](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection/tree/main/configs/experiments)), see [`docs/kaggle_cropandweed.md`](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection/blob/main/docs/kaggle_cropandweed.md) |
| Trained weights | [`models/released/`](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection/tree/main/models/released/) (exp 3–5 and the CottonWeedDet12 model) |
| Validation, selection, test | [`docs/kaggle_validation.md`](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection/blob/main/docs/kaggle_validation.md): [`scripts/evaluate_split.py`](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection/blob/main/scripts/evaluate_split.py), [`scripts/select_model.py`](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection/blob/main/scripts/select_model.py) |
| Site data and gallery | `python scripts/site/export_site_data.py`, [`scripts/site/fetch_sugarbeets_sample.py`](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection/blob/main/scripts/site/fetch_sugarbeets_sample.py), [`scripts/site/make_gallery.py`](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection/blob/main/scripts/site/make_gallery.py) |
| This website | `cd site && quarto render` |
| Analysis notebooks | [`notebooks/`](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection/tree/main/notebooks) (data exploration, model outputs, results analysis) |

Key code: threshold sweep and the 2 % rule in [`src/targeting/sweep.py`](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection/blob/main/src/targeting/sweep.py), model selection in
[`src/selection.py`](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection/blob/main/src/selection.py), aim points in [`src/targeting/points.py`](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection/blob/main/src/targeting/points.py), crop gate in [`src/targeting/safety.py`](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection/blob/main/src/targeting/safety.py), baseline
in [`src/baseline.py`](https://github.com/yuvraj-rathod-1202/weed-detection/blob/main/src/baseline.py).

## My contribution and AI use

This is a solo project: I framed the question, chose the datasets, designed the split, metrics and selection
rule, ran all training and evaluation on Kaggle, and wrote the analysis and this site.

**AI use.** I used **Claude Code** (Anthropic) as a coding assistant throughout: writing and debugging
code (data conversion, training and evaluation scripts, the threshold sweep, the gallery and this website),
analysing results, and drafting text. I reviewed and ran all code myself, checked the key numbers against
the raw outputs, and am responsible for every result and claim on this page. No other AI tools were used.
External code and data are cited below; ultralytics (YOLO11, AGPL-3.0) and SAM 2.1 are used as libraries.
